summary: An informational memo describing the procedures and criteria the IETF Transport Area uses to review reliable multicast protocols, because applications exist that need reliable delivery to many receivers at once.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for judging ways to send the same message to many people so that everyone gets all of it.

questions: why is reliable multicast hard to standardize
subtitle: The checklist the IETF Transport Area said a reliable multicast protocol must pass before it could become an RFC.

tldr.problem: Many applications want reliable delivery to a whole group, but a careless reliable multicast protocol could flood the Internet and cause congestion collapse.
tldr.mechanism: The Transport Area Directors set out review criteria: a draft must analyze scalability, congestion control, error recovery, robustness and security, and back the analysis with trials or simulations.
tldr.outcome: Drafts that meet the criteria default to Experimental status; Standards Track drafts that fail them are not supported, and other drafts may carry an IESG note.

today: RFC 2357 is an Informational memo from June 1998 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It sets out review procedure, not a protocol, and it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: How the Review Works
sections.content:
In the IETF, Area Directors (ADs) direct the work of an area and charter working groups. They also review Internet-Drafts that are submitted individually, not by a working group, before those drafts can be published as RFCs. Reviews follow the Internet Standards Process in RFC 2026.

This memo presents the criteria the Transport Area (TSV) ADs will use for reliable multicast drafts of any RFC type. For a Standards Track draft, failing the criteria means the ADs will decline to support publication, which is enough to stop it. For an Experimental or Informational draft, the ADs will at minimum recommend publishing it with an IESG note saying that the protocol fails to comply with the criteria.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a new idea gets printed in the official rulebook, the referees check it. If it fails the checklist, it either does not get printed or gets printed with a warning label.

sections.title: Why Reliable Multicast Is Different
sections.content:
The memo says there is strong application demand for reliable multicast, for example collaborative tools, distributed virtual reality and software upgrade services. The current Internet multicast model offers best-effort many-to-many delivery with no guarantees. Reliable multicast adds delivery guarantees, not necessarily like those of reliable unicast TCP, to the group-delivery model.

Two things make standardization hard. First, the meaning of reliability varies between applications. Second, without special care these protocols can threaten the operation of the global Internet. Because of this, the memo puts in place review procedures that are more explicit than usual, and compares the step to an earlier IESG action in 1991 on routing protocols (RFC 1264).
sections.plainLanguage: Sending to a whole crowd is much harder than sending to one friend. Different crowds also want different things from the word reliable, and a sloppy method can clog the roads for everybody.

sections.title: One Protocol or Many?
sections.content:
For unicast, one transport protocol, TCP, serves a wide range of applications. Reliable multicast does not necessarily lend itself to a single interface or a single set of mechanisms. Applications differ on whether delivery needs a total ordering, whether many members or only one source send data, whether data is replicated so several members can transmit it, how large and how dynamic the group is (small fixed groups versus thousands or tens of thousands of members), how strict the delay requirements are, and how much bandwidth is used.

Some applications will even trade less than complete reliability for more timely delivery. The memo notes general agreement that a single reliable multicast protocol or framework is unlikely to meet every need, but less agreement on how application requirements map onto generic underlying mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: A group chat, a file download for a whole class and a live whiteboard all need different things. One tool probably cannot be perfect for all of them.

sections.title: The Congestion Problem
sections.content:
The IETF's central worry is the effect of reliable multicast traffic on competing TCP traffic during congestion. The Internet depends on best-effort traffic reducing its load when links are congested, and congestion collapse is prevented only by the congestion control built into TCP (see RFC 2001).

The memo gives reasons multicast deserves extra care. One multicast flow can spread along a large global tree. Unreliable audio and video usually have a person watching who will leave the group if the stream becomes unintelligible, but reliable group file transfer runs between computers with no human watching. Such a transfer may also continue until every receiver has all the data, so a flow has potentially unlimited duration, and ACKs, NACKs and status messages can add a complex explosion of control traffic.

The stated challenge is to encourage research and implementation while protecting the Internet from the congestion disaster that inadequate mechanisms could cause if widely used.
sections.plainLanguage: If a thousand computers all keep shouting until everyone has heard, and none of them ever slows down, the road jams for everyone. A person would give up and leave, but a computer will not.

sections.title: Technical Criteria for Drafts
sections.content:
Section 5 of the memo says the Internet-Draft must, in itself or a companion draft, meet these requirements.

  • Analyze behavior. Show vulnerabilities and performance problems through analysis, explaining scalability, congestion control, error recovery and robustness. Congestion control that is more aggressive than TCP faces a great burden of proof that it does not threaten network stability.
  • Trials or simulations. Describe trials or simulations that support the design and the answers above.
  • Congestion avoidance. Analyze whether the protocol can cope with the global Internet, and if not, document the circumstances in which congestion harm can occur and how to prevent them.
  • Containment. Describe any mechanisms that confine traffic to limited network environments, noting that confinement is an open research area.
  • Security and privacy. Analyze each mode of secure operation, say which parties (senders, forwarders, receivers, retransmission sources) must be trusted, and ask whether data can be manipulated so some receivers get different copies.

For retransmission, the presumption is that either congestion control inherently limits retransmission traffic and holds up under concerted attack, or retransmission requests are signed cryptographically so abuse can be traced to its source. Protocols with neither face a great burden of proof. Drafts must also address what key management the protocol requires and provides.
sections.plainLanguage: The checklist asks: will it still work when the crowd gets huge, will it slow down when the road is full, did you test it, and can a bad actor cheat? You have to show your work.

sections.title: From Draft to RFC
sections.content:
Under RFC 2026, ADs may bring a closely related individual draft into the IETF, or recommend publishing it as Experimental or Informational, with or without an IESG annotation. For reliable multicast, the default RFC status is Experimental once the technical criteria are deemed fulfilled. The memo says the criteria reflect the ADs' technical assessment of the state of the technology, not where proposals come from, which it expects to be equally commercial vendors and researchers.

Development work could happen in the IRTF Reliable Multicast Research Group or a focused short IETF working group with an Experimental product. Once the technology matures, the TSV Area may charter working groups for Standards Track documents, and the criteria for those will be at least as stringent. The memo also says a few earlier RFCs, RFC 1301 and RFC 1458, were published before the congestion impact was fully appreciated and should be deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: New ideas start as experiments. Only after they prove themselves can they graduate to a real standard, and the bar for that is even higher.
